questions.title: Redis Caching in Spring Boot
questions.question: How do you integrate Redis caching in a Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@Cacheable`, `@CacheEvict`, `@CachePut`: Spring cache abstraction**
- **Cache-aside: application loads from cache, falls back to DB on miss**
- **TTL (Time-To-Live): auto-expire stale data — always set TTL in production**
- **Cache invalidation: hardest problem — evict on update or use short TTL**
- **Redis beyond cache: sessions, rate limiting, pub/sub, distributed locks**
- **Don't cache everything: cache read-heavy, infrequently-changed, expensive-to-compute data**

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Redis is the most popular caching layer for Java backends. Spring Boot's cache abstraction lets you add caching to service methods with simple annotations: `@Cacheable` caches the result on the first call and returns the cached value on subsequent calls with the same arguments. `@CacheEvict` removes entries when data changes. This abstraction works with Redis, Caffeine, or any other cache provider without changing business code.

The most important operational concern is TTL. Always set a time-to-live on cached values — without it, stale data can live in the cache indefinitely, causing subtle bugs that are hard to reproduce. The TTL should balance freshness requirements against DB load reduction.

Redis is also used for more than caching: distributed session storage, rate limiting counters, distributed locks with Redisson, and pub/sub messaging. Understanding these secondary use cases shows depth.
